The daughter is on the phone with a kidnapper who is holding her friend hostage and demanding ¥100 million delivered alone by noon, with no police. The father is under surveillance by the kidnapper's group and cannot go himself, so if the ransom were paid, the daughter would be the one forced to bring the money alone to the kidnapper. The father realizes that once the daughter delivered the money she would see the kidnapper's face and could identify him, so the kidnapper would kill her to silence her as a witness. Although he cares about the hostage, paying the ransom would thus put the daughter's own life in grave danger, so he decides the ransom should not be paid—choosing to protect his daughter rather than let her walk into the trap.

The daughter is the person the kidnapper is negotiating with directly over the smartphone. The hostage is someone she knows personally, but not her lover, boyfriend, or close friend, and the father genuinely cares about the hostage and does not want the hostage to die. The ransom demand itself is ¥100 million, brought alone by noon with no police.

The father refuses to pay because he reasons about what paying would entail. If the ransom were paid, the daughter—the one dealing directly with the kidnapper—would be the person who personally goes to hand over the money to him. In doing so she would come face to face with the kidnapper and see his face, making her able to identify him. The kidnapper would then likely kill her to eliminate her as a witness. The father therefore fears that paying the ransom would put his daughter's own life at grave risk.

Even though refusing may not save the hostage, the father chooses to refuse so that the daughter is not sent to deliver the money and into the danger of being killed. His decision is driven not by any inability of his own or by a belief that the hostage would be saved, but by a determination to protect the daughter from walking into the trap.

The daughter is speaking directly with the kidnapper over the smartphone; he is holding hostage someone she knows personally and demands ¥100 million brought alone by noon, with no police. The father overhears the demand and genuinely does not want the hostage to die, but he refuses to pay.

The reason lies in what paying would set in motion. If the ransom were paid, it would be the daughter—the one dealing directly with the kidnapper—who would personally go to hand over the money. By delivering it she would come face to face with the kidnapper and see his face, leaving her able to identify him; she would then be at grave risk of being killed to silence her as a witness. The father's fear is for the daughter's own life in this delivery, not a belief that the ransom is futile or that refusing saves the hostage (he does not think the hostage will survive without payment). Nor is his decision motivated by any inability of his own or by surveillance, which is irrelevant to the choice.

So although paying might nominally serve the hostage, the father concludes the ransom should not be paid because doing so would send his daughter into the kidnapper's hands, where seeing his face would likely cost her her life. He chooses to keep her from walking into that trap rather than to pay.
